Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself in some measure with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) in regard to his attitude respecting private business of the country, and I would support, too, much that has been said by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). It must be laid down as a fundamental principle upon which all our thinking and acting must be based that this country must be made safe for industry. It must be made such that industry can thrive and increase throughout the land.
One point which fills me with anxiety regarding the minister's whole tax structure- and I say this nqt without sympathy for him in the difficulties with which he is faced-is that practically every move is along lines which make industry more difficult. It is impossible for me to see how the country can be great and strong unless its industries are great and strong.
I said the other night, and I shall now repeat, that not only must industries abound throughout the country, but small industries must have a chance.

They will not, so long as it
is not safe.

I believe these restrictions and taxes are tending to destroy smaller industries for the benefit of the larger ones, which means that there will develop in Canada a centralization of industry that in due time will result in suffering, misery and frustration which to-day it is impossible to foresee.
It may be asked: How would you get along without these taxes? It is possible to get along without them, but it is not in order at this time that I set forth the ways in which that can be done. Several times in past years I have risen in my place in the house and endeavoured to set forth those principles. The majority of hon. members apparently have taken the view that I was wrong before I started, and that consequently nothing could be learned from me. I am, however, telling hon. members now that they are going to learn by experience which will be bitter beyond the greatest bitterness ever experienced in Canada, unless they begin to become somewhat broader in their thinking, and unless they begin to realize that money can be obtained without taxation which will destroy the very basis of our life, namely, our goods and services producing power.
In the closing days of the session I would urge that the minister set about at once, with his experts, to find a way of relieving the people of Canada of a large measure of the onerous taxation he has imposed upon them

since the beginning of the war. If he has not upon his staff experts who can tell him how to do that, then I humbly suggest to him that he procure other experts. There are such men to be found in this world. I protest against the burdensome, devastating, disintegrating taxation which has been placed upon the people of Canada by the operations of the budget introduced this year.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on this particular bill, but I was interested in the remarks of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). I know he has devoted a good deal of time to a consideration of this legislation, and I tried to follow him as closely as possible. I think we all realize that money must be raised in some way. Just a few moments before this motion was put we approved amendments to the Pension Act, and no doubt at the next session we shall be considering amendments to the War Veterans' Allowance Act. Money must be raised with which to carry on these services, to say nothing at all of the expenditures occasioned by our direct war endeavours.
The question has been raised as to whether this is a direct tax upon capital. I submit that no one has an inalienable right to transmit property to his descendants. The natural law is that a man should part with his property at the time of his death. The fact that dependents or relatives are entitled to come into possession of his estate is wholly dependent upon the laws of the country and the facilities that are provided for the administration of estates. We have heard something this afternoon of the hardship that will be imposed upon an estate made up largely of good-will or other business assets. After observing estates for many years, my experience is that considerable money is lost by neglecting to dispose of assets shortly after the death of a business man. Many times an estate is allowed to remain in abeyance and is disposed of a considerable time afterwards when conditions have changed. Instead of a hoped for improvement in business having occurred, many times it is found that a serious depreciation has taken place and the estate is forced to suffer a considerable loss.
This tax may not be as equitable a tax as the income tax, but we cannot raise all the money required by income taxation. I suppose this tax is really a modified capital tax in the sense that part of an estate is taken in the form of taxation. We are, however, faced with an emergency, and I think capital should be prepared to make a modest contribution or concession. Otherwise forces that exist in this country to-day may destroy capital. We are not considering this matter

Succession Duty Act-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford)
on the basis of an ideal set of circumstances; we are faced with certain facts. The statement was made by President Grover Cleveland many years ago and often repeated in this house that what we have to face is a condition, not a theory. There is no doubt that taxes are distasteful to all of us; nobody likes the surgeon who comes to cut him up. In order, however, to keep our national life going, we must have taxes. I think in all the circumstances that this tax does not invade the provincial field too greatly, as has been suggested. It is a reasonable tax and one quite attunable to present conditions. I may have a word to say with respect to one or two details when we are discussing the bill in committee, but at this stage I merely wish to express my complete concurrence in the bill.

Mr. Speaker, before we go into
committee I should like to express briefly my views on this bill. I do not consider that this is an invasion of provincial rights. The fact that the dominion has not taken advantage of this form of taxation in the past does not mean that it did not have the right to do so. I find myself to some extent in accord with the points raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) with regard to the effect upon incentive. We are getting near to the point in connection with taxation where we shall discourage people who otherwise would bring advantages to this country through their energy. We are inspired to make efforts by two things: first, in order to help the state and mankind generally, but I am afraid that this is not always enough. There must be a certain amount of profit incentive, and if we take away all the profit we are likely to destroy that incentive.
Our forefathers came to this country from the lands beyond the seas because they felt that there were greater opportunities here, not only for themselves but for their children and their children's children. Those opportunities were here for them and for their children, and we must make sure that they will still be here for their children's children. They were hemmed in in the old land; they could not advance and improve their positions in the world.

That is not why they
left.

My hon. friend says that that is not why they left, but I suggest that that is one reason why many of our forefathers left the old land. They wanted to have greater opportunities for themselves, for their children and for their children's children. They did advance themselves; they brought much happiness to
themselves and to those who came after them. We must be energetic and full of enterprise, but if all profit is to be taken away I am just afraid we shall not have the same enterprise and enthusiasm. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has said that industry must be great and strong.
I can go that far with him, but I cannot agree that the theories which he advances will make industry great and strong. I am afraid that they will have the opposite effect.
This bill is introduced for the purpose of raising money for this war.
It is not confined to that.

The leader of the opposition says it is not confined to that. We do not know. Only the future will tell. At the present time we need and must have money to obtain equipment of all kinds to supply our fighting forces.
The minister does not agree with that.
I am sure the minister will agree with that.
I do not know.

I am expressing my view, and I have found myself at most times in accord with the minister. We must have all the necessary supplies to ' defeat the enemy, and we must have the wherewithal to get those supplies. This is one of the means whereby we can get the money to purchase those supplies. I have not had one objection from my district against this tax or any other tax which has been put into effect by this budget. Everyone is in accord with the idea; raise the money-we are prepared to pay-give the troops what they need in order to win. If this tax is going to help in any way to do that-and I am sure it is'-then I am in complete accord with it and with every tax which is imposed for that purpose.
My only warning, Mr. Speaker, is this. Let us not forget that this country has become great under the system which has been in effect here, where a person who works gets a reward and the reward is not all taken from him. I am confident that Canada can go forward in the future, after this war is over, only if we continue that system. Let the worker be worthy of his hire, and let us not take all his earnings from him.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the principle of this bill-perhaps something unusual for me. So long, however, as the wealth and natural resources of this country can pass, as they do

Succession Duty Act-Mr. Castleden
now, through corporate organizations into the hands of a few people, thereby preventing large numbers of labouring people from exchanging their labour for decent standards of living, there must be some form of taxation whereby the wealth that to-day accumulates in the hands of a comparatively few, can be drawn back into the coffers of the nation. It is because this bill institutes such machinery in the federal field that I rise to support it in principle. It is only through such means as this that we can prevent the complete domination of this country by wealth and power.
Statements have been made this afternoon that taxation of this sort kills initiative. I take exception to that. I do not know of anything that is more deadening to initiative than to compel over one million people to live on relief. When labour cannot be found, initiative dies. I am afraid there have not been enough people in this house in close enough contact with those who have not been able to find work, and who know what a degenerating effect it has upon any man to be unable to provide for his wife and his loved ones, to find himself trapped so that no matter where he looks he cannot find work to provide for those whom he loves and desires to protect. Take the case of a young man wishing to start out in life and finding no opportunity, who finally comes to look upon himself as an unwanted member of society. If you want to kill initiative, that is the way to do it, and that lis what has been happening in Canada, a young nation, for far, far too long, for far, far too many people.
That is what made Hitler in Germany.

Somebody said a short time ago that no nation can be healthy which is not healthy industrially. I agree, but there should not be that degree of control which industry has maintained over the lives of the people of this country. It should not be possible for large corporations and big concerns through cutthroat competition gradually to kill small business and prevent competition. Yet that is what they do. They employ labour from an overflowing labour market and drive the price of labour down to a point at which a man can scarcely make a living-drive labour at whatever speed they wish to, drive it until everything that is good within them is ruined, and then labour is cast out on the ash-heap of humanity and the employer takes no responsibility, the one motive behind the whole organization being nothing but profits and dividends-how their stock will stand in the stock market-with no concern for the humanitarian side of it. That profit motive 
must go. Apparently at the present time we are not in a state where we can drive that motive out entirely, but if this measure creates a check upon that kind of expansion in industry, and if it will do anything towards preventing too large an expansion of these big corporations and the wealth of individuals-
Corporations never die.
Unfortunately that is so. They also have no heart and no soul.
And they breed nazism.

The next step from a national organization of industry is the international organization; and when you get that form, which spreads its control over the whole world, you are bound to 'have trouble.
Under the system we now have, this type of taxation should not only be brought in, but be extended, and I believe that it will be extended very largely. I am glad to support the principle of this bill.

speechtext: The hon. member is right on a fundamental and important point of principle. I had to explain that point once before, and I do not know whether I did it very well or fully.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member for Brantford City raised the same point; only he made a much more flagrant case of discrimination, if I might use that word. He took an estate of $5,000,000 and compared it with an estate of $25,000. But this feature is found in all the provincial acts.

On the
theory that they would get more money; there is no doubt about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, not necessarily. It
depends altogether upon the rates. If hon. members will bear with me for a moment,
I shall explain the law as best I can.
There are three types of succession, death or estate duties acts. There is the straight estate duty which is a duty on the estate

Succession Duty Act
graded in proportion to the estate, the rate proportion rising as the amount of the estate rises. That would be a graduated estate duty. There were those who thought that the Dominion of Canada should adopt that form of death or estate duty. It is very easy to administer; it does not require the valuing of contingent interests. The commissioner of income tax told me he thought he could almost administer it with his existing staff, if we were to adopt the simple estate duty. But that is much more unjust than the measure before the committee, if the element which the hon. member has mentioned is an element of injustice, because then, out of an estate of $100,000, perhaps 10 per cent would come off, and we would get $10,000 from the estate, regardless of whether it goes to ten people or to one person, and also regardless of the relationship. That would be a straight estate duty. In that instance the government is coming in and taxing the estate. It is taxing the small estate at a small rate, the larger estate at a larger rate and the big estate at a high rate, having no regard whatsoever to the amount going to any individual.

And
irrespective of the incidence of the tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, irrespective of the
incidence of the tax on individuals. There are those who argue strongly that that is perfectly just, because they say that a succession duty is not like an income tax, where one ascertains what the entire income of a person is, and then grades his tax in accordance with his ability to pay. The $25,000 legatee may have had tremendous ability to pay. He may have been a millionaire, or he may have had nothing. We do not know about that. We do not go into that field at all.
There are those who say that we should look just at the estate, and take part of the estate of those who die, a larger part of a large estate and a smaller part of a small estate. That would be a graduated estate tax.
There are those who hold the contrary view, namely, that we should have a pure succession duty act, and that in such a measure we should perhaps tax purely in accordance with the amount received, so that the man who received $25,000 from a $5,000,000 estate would pay exactly the same tax as the man who received $25,000 from a $25,000 estate. That would be a pure succession duty act, and there may be pure succession duty acts in some parts of the world. There were those among my advisers who argued for that style of tax.
We decided finally not to take either one, but to do just what the provinces have done,
and to combine the two forms of taxation. Therefore this is partly an estate duty and partly a succession duty.
Will the minister tell us why the provinces have been actuated to do that, and why he was so actuated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because it is a compromise between the two principles. It adopts one element of each principle. I might branch into another realm, one which will be very provocative, I am afraid, and for that reason I am foolish to mention it. I have heard it argued that a person who reoeived $25,000 from a $100,000 estate is likely to be able to bear a heavier tax than a person who received $25,000 from a $25,000 estate. It is argued that if a person is a beneficiary from a large estate, he is likely to have had benefits in his lifetime, to have lived in circles and to have had expenditures upon him and for his benefit -advantages in education, and that sort of thing-which would render him better able to bear a heavy tax on the $25,000 legacy he would get than the person receiving a similar legacy on a smaller estate.
It seems to me that is pretty far-fetched.

That is only
supposition.
It is an assumption.
What is the third type to which the minister referred?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The third type is what we call the provincial model, a combination of the estate duty and the succession duty.

Is the
provincial model not based on the theory that by a combination of the two types they will get more money from deaths? Is that not the basis of this bill, and of the provincial acts? Section 5 states that "the duty payable by each successor shall not be subject to any increase or decrease by reason of appreciation or depreciation in the value of the property included in a succession after the date of death". Naturally it would be a difficult section if worded otherwise. On the other hand, I am sure the minister is acquainted with some cases, and I can recall one particularly in Ontario where on paper a man was worth several millions of dollars, but by the time the estate got round to probate it was worth only a few hundred thousand dollars. That occurs fairly frequently.
For instance, a fortune rapidly created is usually created because very heavy risks were undertaken. It may be that the tide of fortune may turn quickly against that particular estate, and it becomes worth only a fraction of its former value. This would seem to prevent any discretion whatsoever not only in the department or in the minister, but any other place. It is mandatory that there shall be no change whatsoever, no matter what the hardship may be. I believe in the larger brackets there are sufficient cases which are really worthy of attention, and with regard to which some clemency might properly be granted. What are the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act? We sometimes hear that the provisions of that act are related to extreme cases of hardship.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It authorizes the governor in council to remit duties and taxes.
Generally, where there is a hardship?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For any reason, or for no reason; it just authorizes the governor in council to remit them.

Would it not be possible to have a provision here to cover such cases? I could cite the case I have in mind where such circumstances had arisen. There are times when it is utterly impossible to pay duties when the value of the estate has crumbled. We have seen values crumble once in the last decade, and it is quite possible that they may be built up fictitiously again. Should a man happen to die at the very zenith of these values, and probate of the estate is taken in six months or a year, it may happen that his widow will be left with nothing, in fact be in debt to the department. I should think some provision might be made to cover these special cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the Consolidated
Revenue and Audit Act is sufficient. Instead of putting a provision in this bill at the outset, I think it would be better to see what our experience is. If there should happen to be glaring cases and it is felt that they cannot be dealt with under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, then perhaps we can amend this measure. We have the power under another act, a power which is exercised right along in certain classes of cases.

This is an overriding
act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That has no reference to the remission of duties.
So long as it is permissive, it will be satisfactory.

The question has been raised as to the actual date of fixing the value for succession duty purposes. I believe in Ontario the date of death is taken. It may happen that an estate is made up of stock which is fluctuating on the market, and a beneficiary may not receive his bequest for as long as three years after the death of the testator. He certainly could not get it for at least from thirty days to six months. Some consideration should be given to that class of asset. Considerable increases or decreases may occur in the values, and it would be more fair and equitable if a date were taken nearer to the time the beneficiary received the bequest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That would be something entirely new if we fixed a date at some time after death. Since this measure combines the

elements of an estate duty and a succession duty, I do not think any date is more appropriate than the date of death. It is the most logical of any date that could be suggested.
I agree with that.
Would the minister be kind enough to give the definition of "domicile" as used in this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has a common law meaning. I cannot define "domicile" in a word. If I remember correctly, there are Latin phrases such as animus manendi, animus revertendi, and so forth. The subject is tremendously complicated. "Domicile" is covered by a definite branch of the law; there is a vast body of law upon the matter.
The definition is not clear to me, but perhaps that is due to the fact that I am not legal minded. I should like to know what "domicile" or "resident of" means.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: "Residence" is not the same as "domicile"; "residence" is an element of "domicile", but it is only one element. Books have been written on this.

The remarks which have been made in the last two or three minutes indicate the need for the information for which I asked. It now appears that books have been written on the matter, and evidently there is a great divergence of opinion in this chamber. There is no more important word in the whole bill. The disposition of money and other matters will depend upon the meaning of the word "domicile". Surely this is the place to arrive at some definition which the ordinary, common man can understand. Perhaps it is unfortunate that the constitution of Canada does not provide that every member of parliament shall be a lawyer, but since we are not all lawyers I think the ordinary country man or the business man from the small town is entitled to know just what we are passing. We shall have to go home and explain this to people who are not lawyers, and I should think one of the most important things to be done is to define the word which is the very crux of this bill. I know of a recent case where a man had left the old country forty-four years ago. When he died a few months ago, it was discovered that he
had left a few hundred pounds in Britain,
[DOT] and the question arose as to whether he had been domiciled in Canada. It was alleged by a lawyer of some ability that it might be held that he was domiciled in the country of his birth, that he had come to Canada with the view of ultimately returning to the country of his birth. I think some information should be given to the ordinary member to indicate what "domicile" really does mean.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

Perhaps I could give
hon. gentlemen	my recollection of a
few of the rules relating to domicile. There is the domicile of origin, and then there is the domicile of choice. That is probably the country where a person comes to live, with the intention of staying, not the country in which he was born. But as soon as he begins to drift, the domicile of origin reverts, and even though he is not physically present in the country of origin, he is considered as being domiciled there. I may be wrong about that because it is a most complicated subject. If I were to insert a definition of "domicile" that would cover all the variations, domicile of origin, domicile of choice, and so forth, it would be a very long one. A dictionary definition cannot be inserted. We mean the legal definition of "domicile," which the courts know all about.

It would appear that the

Do I understand

speechtext: I will give the hon. gentleman a dictionary definition.

I agree entirely with the
minister that it would be a grave mistake for us to attempt to put a statutory definition of the word "domicile" into this bill. If the
Succession Duty Act

hon. member for Chilliwack-no, Fraser Valley-they are both very delightful places,' I have been there recently-will accept a suggestion from me, "domicile" is worked out in this way. It is, in cases, said to be determined almost entirely as a question of intention in the mind of the person whose domicile is being inquired into, and that is sometimes a pretty difficult matter to determine.
The question arises frequently in connection with foreign divorces and has to be passed on by our courts. To illustrate, if a man resident in Ontario goes to Nevada for from three to six months and purports to make his residence there, whether it be humble or in a flashy hotel, then applies to the court in connection with divorce, and then returns to Canada and takes up again his residence or his business where he was before, it has been argued that when he went to Nevada he created a domicile there. British courts and Canadian courts will have none of that. They look behind the mere fact of residence for a period short or long and attempt to determine, from whatever evidence may be brought forward in an individual case, whether it was the intention of the man in the case I have mentioned, for instance, to desert his domicile of origin, as the minister outlined, and take out a permanent, real, definite residence in some other place for the rest of his life and, unless something unforeseen occurs to alter his intention, to reside at the place where he is found at the time of his death. That is the nearest I can get to what "domicile" is. There is a great deal of legal lore on the subject, and for us here to attempt to define it will,
I am afraid, create difficulty, whereas, if my hon. friend will have faith in the department and in the working out of the legislation in any particular case, I think there will be no difficulty with domicile.
It is said that some wealthy Canadians have disappeared from Canada and gone to a foreign jurisdiction in order to escape the succession duties. If they should die away from Canada we would have the right to inquire whether their business abroad was of a temporary nature or whether their real and honest intention was to create a new home in a foreign jurisdiction for all time to come, subject to the right to change their mind, bona fide, later on. I have probably beclouded rather than cleared the issue.

Since the question of domicile has come up, may I say that I was bom in Sweden, of which I am very proud. I left Sweden some forty years ago as an able seaman to go to any country where I thought I might like to take up my domicile. I came to the United States of America and became a citizen of that country, but I decided that I had not yet found the place where I was ready to establish my permanent domicile. I had read a certain amount about the British tradition of justice and fair play, and I decided to come to Canada. I was married in Canada in 1909, and I have one son and one daughter. My son is in the air force. My son-in-law is in the Canadian army. I myself happen to be too old. May I add that when the former Minister of Finance suggested that British people should finance this war, I said to him, "If you are going to conscript blood you should conscript wealth, and I have a few dollars to dispose of." I do not think we should go into these fine technicalities about "domicile." I have tried to be a Canadian and a Britisher, and I am probably the only one in this House of Commons who has offered everything I have-my son, my son-in-law and my daughter-and I have a grandson of whom I am very proud. I think it is ridiculous to be discussing these technicalities at the present time when we should be doing all we can to win this war.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley is a returned soldier from the last war, and I think he should appreciate this, that when we are all trying to do the best we can in this conflict that we are up against, it is out of order to question anyone's domicile. Let me assure you, Mr. Chairman, and the committee that I am a Canadian, first, last and all the time, and I stand for that fairness, justice and equality for which we are all fighting.

With regard to section 6, following the argument of the hon. member for Rosedale, I might give an illustration which may possibly be contemplated in this provision, namely, the case of such corporations as the Canadian Pacific Railway, which hold property in other countries than Canada. It cannot be said to be entirely a Canadian corporation if there are transfer agents in different places. There are three or four propositions that might be raised under provincial acts. Succession Duty Act

is also a consideration. The actual property of which the certificate is simply a representation cannot be the whole ratio decidendi. speechtext: I do not know whether a question was asked. I know that sometimes it is difficult to determine what the situs of personal property is. That is
quite true where there is more than one registration office. It is an anomalous situation, and I do not think one jurisdiction can settle it without collaboration with the other. The principle set up, namely, that they cannot be effectively dealt with-I think those are the words of the English decision-is based on the theory set up in England a long time ago in respect of shares and followed right down to the present time. It has worked great hardship. Just because there is a place where you can register and unregister, therefore you must pay taxation there although the shares were bought in Canada or the United States and never saw England except for the purpose of registration. It is just a hook to catch the money as it goes through.
The same thing occurs in connection with the registration, in a city like Montreal, of shares or bonds, of, say, a New Brunswick corporation. The stock exchange requirements are that the register must be kept in a convenient place where the shares can be dealt with quickly. Under that theory, shares in a New Brunswick company must be registered in Montreal even if the company's operations are wholly in New Brunswick, and one has to pay the province of Quebec succession duty before he can have the shares released. That, of course, and the situation visualized here in respect of registration in other places, such as New York, are very unfair. Of course, under this measure it cannot happen with respect to Canadian registration, because this is a federal statute; but I have always felt TMr. Boucher.]
that the theory upon which those decisions are based was not applicable to a country like Canada.

In the case of the $35,000

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The expression "active service" means something, surely.

May I draw the minister's attention to an answer given by the Minister of National Defence and reported at page 2908 of Hansard? If the minister will look up that page he will see that included in the active service force are the veterans guard, the coast defence and anti-aircraft units, and the instructional staffs and training centres.
I do not know if that is what the Minister of Finance has in mind; but if he is going to let this section stand I would draw his attention particularly to what was said on that occasion by the Minister of National Defence. [DOT]

If the word "active" were deleted and the word "service" remained, then in the event of the regular army being called up for two weeks military training and a man being killed in that time, his estate would be exempt from the provisions of this measure.
Only if he came under the Pension Act.
I do not think that is the intention of the legislation. I believe its intention is to give special consideration-
Not "special"-equitable, probably.

It is a consideration over and above that given to a person who does not go to war. It is to ;ive consideration to those who offered their lives for their country. If they are killed while offering their lives for their country, then they are to get the extra consideration which this section sets out. I do not think the section is intended to mean that benefits shall be given to anyone who happens to be killed during two weeks military training.

I do not agree with the hon. member for Brantford City. If a man is killed while he is on military training in Canada,
he is dead, just the same as if he were killed overseas, and his family would find themselves in just the same sort of trouble. It is frightfully difficult under the pension law as it stands to-day for a man serving in Canada, even though he may be waiting to go overseas, to qualify for pension. It is frightfully difficult for his widow to qualify for pension. That is what we were complaining about yesterday. We pointed out that some wider provision should be made for men who are in active training for overseas service. But, as the law stands now, it will be very difficult for a man to qualify.
I submit to the minister that if a widow can qualify on the death of her husband, then certainly that should be a case in which she should be entitled to this exemption, which, after all, starts at quite a high figure. I think, if we start drawing fine lines, we shall only be unfair. A man's life is offered for his country if it is given for his country here in Canada. He is a member of our forces, and his family should be entitled to the benefit of this exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: As the section stands, it is clear. According to the interpretation of the officers of the national defence department it includes everyone in Canada, except those called out under the National Resources Mobilization Act. They are all on active service or on service within or without Canada. Therefore this section applies to all, if they could qualify for pension under the Pension Act as passed by the house-and if not modified in another place. That would be the interpretation of the section as it stands to-day.

It seems to me most
reasonable that if a person is entitled to pension he should be entitled to exemption, and, conversely, if he is entitled to exemption he should be entitled to pension. Therefore I believe it simply follows that one should be the test for the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Are hon. members arguing that in a time of peace all the privileges of this section should extend to men whose deaths take place while they are training?

Yes, because under those
conditions it is very difficult for a man's dependents to qualify for pension. There would be very few cases which would arise; and if a man has given his life for Canada, even though it may have been in peace time, he has given it as a result of preparing to defend his country in war time. Surely we are drawing too fine a line when we say that in those circumstances the widow is not entitled to the exemption.
Succession Duty Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just a moment; I have asked a question for information. Are hon. members arguing that a man who loses his life while training in time of peace, who has not volunteered for service for any war abroad, should be treated differently as regards succession duties from the man who does not train in a summer camp?

If a man gives his life
while he is out training to defend his country he has the right I have described. I would urge upon the minister that we cannot get away from the Pension Act. He must base his section in the succession duties legislation on the provisions of the Pension Act. Otherwise it will be like a ship without a rudder. There would be no way of determining what active service is.

The minister has asked for the opinions of hon. members. I dio not' believe that a man who in peace time goes to military camp for two weeks training should get the benefit of this section. He has not offered his life in any way for his country. True, he joined a militia unit-and no one has more respect for the militia units than I have-but he has not offered himself for service outside Canada. He has only offered to take two weeks training at a military camp. I do not believe such a man should receive the benefits of this section. I agree that a man who, in time of war, volunteers for service, joins a unit that is likely to go overseas, and is killed in Canada, should get the benefit of this measure. The minister has asked for our opinions, and I am definitely not in favour of giving pension to men who are called for two weeks training only in Canada.

Does the hon.
member believe that the. pension law is wrong, and that a man should not receive a pension under the conditions the hon. member has mentioned?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: He can.

Under the Pension Act as it is drawn, and as it passed this house yesterday, there is provision for a man who is killed during two weeks service. There is provision that his wife shall receive a pension.

I do not understand the hon. member's argument at all. In one case the man is getting a tremendous benefit, and in the other, his widow is getting a very small benefit. In the case of the Succession Duty Act the benefit is very small, when compared with the pension which would be received.

I suggest that the hon. member should be consistent and argue that the Pension Act as now drafted is wrong, and that the man is not entitled to pension. I suggest that the consideration for the exemption must be the pension. It should not be anything else; the pension is really the consideration.

As the bill is now drawn, the obtaining of the benefits of the section are dependent upon active service, and a pension. That is the intention of the legislation. I do not think we should widen it, and give benefit to those who do nothing but take two weeks training.

I suggest that
the hon. member ought to be consistent. He is arguing against the man getting a pension under the conditions he has set out. I do not see how it can be otherwise. I really believe that the consideration must be the pension.

There would be perhaps only one case a year, or one in two or three years in the militia, where a man would be killed while in training. It would not be a matter of involving the country in a great loss of revenue. The principle should be that if a man's widow can establish entitlement to a pension, she should have the right to exemption under the Succession Duty Act.
Mr. CRUICKSHANIv:	Apparently the
hon. member for Vancouver South is in favour of giving a member who stubs his toe in the Jackson building here a government pension.

The hon. member for Fraser Valley could not have had both his ears open. As he knows very well, a member in the Jackson building could not qualify for a pension. His widow would have to show that the death arose out of his service or was directly attributable to his service. If he stubbed his toe, his widow could not qualify.
If he stubbed his toe, he could qualify if we took the interpretation of the hon. member for Vancouver South.

When I raised the question I was thinking of two fliers from my riding who were killed recently. Perhaps hon. members will remember the accident near Winnipeg in which two fliers were killed, and the other one near lake Erie where another two were killed. In each case one of the men resided in my riding. I do not know whether they were married; but if we assume that they were, their widows should qualify under this provision. I believe one man was an instructor and the other was finishing his training.

Succession Duty Act

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They would be entitled to pensions because their deaths were directly connected with their service.

It seems to
me that there are two criteria by which a person can qualify for exemption. The first is a matter of active service, which is perfectly clear, but the second is a stipulation that there must be eligibility for pension. The Minister of Pensions and National ^ Health may be able to straighten this out. When we consider subsection 3 of section 6 of the Pension Act, we realize that the two are not synonymous any longer. The question of necessitous circumstances now enters the picture. Pensions are now granted not only because of active service but because of the circumstances of the widow. There are now two criteria in the same section, and it seems to me that either one should be used. It should apply either to the active service or to the eligibility for pension.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: When a case of hardship was being considered under the Pension Act, there would be no estate involved. The applicable section would be subsection 2, which covers a death directly connected with military service. The whole trouble is that the meaning of "active service" has completely changed since the last war. During the last war a certain interpretation was placed upon this, and in this war an interpretation has been placed upon it by responsible officers. A man may be called out under the National Resources Mobilization Act, and he is not on active service. I think the intention of this section was to restrict it to those serving in a theatre of war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This was drawn to effectuate the intentions of the government. When we enlist a man and put him in a position of danger, my idea was that we could not fairly subject his estate to succession duties upon the old basis of exemptions or the old basis of value. Therefore the values are greatly reduced on an actuarial basis and the exemptions are greatly increased. I do not know what wording is necessaiy to effect that end, but I know there was no intention of making any concession to men on technical grounds simply because they were wearing a uniform in the summer or anything like that. It is all right to say that it will not cost us very much, that we should not draw fine lines, but we must do the just thing. When we tax one man who does not go to camp, on one basis, and another man who goes to camp, on another basis, and there is not any substantial difference in the risk run by the two men-
Except that the one man gets killed and the other does not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Probably they both get killed.

The man who is killed at
camp is on military service. Surely his position is different?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no difference in the risk, so far as I can see. I want this to cover the cases where we are making concessions to men who are fighting and risking their lives to defend us.

I think it is contradictory. As the Minister of Pensions and National Health points out, it is difficult to understand. I do not think the section means just what the minister wants it to mean. It is an absolute contradiction to what was discussed in connection with the Pension Act last night.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall ask that it stand.
I resent the use of the word "concessions".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I withdraw that; I did not intend anything by it.

The same consideration
should be given to the widows of officers and men who serve in our merchant marine. In some cases these men have been running greater risks than many of the men in our armed forces. They have rendered a great service to this country, and I ask that this section be amended by adding a clause to provide for the officers and men in our merchant marine.
Only if they are killed in a war zone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall give that some
consideration.

If subsection 3 is to stand, may I refer again to the $5,000 limitation? I think the minister will find that the cost of collection will be relatively high. I have urged this matter three times, and the minister has never actually said no. His silence, however, may be construed in that way. In a country as wide-flung as Canada there are bound to be hundreds of little estates where it will be difficult to ascertain whether they come within this limitation. The department will be reduced to counting spoons on the cupboard or in the kitchen to determine whether the estate comes within this limitation. I think the minister ought to raise it to $20,000 at the very least, and I do not think the loss in taxation would be very great. I can remember
Succession Duty Act

that when I first began to practise, $50,000 was the limit. Forty years ago in our province a man with an estate of $50,000 was considered as having been well to do. That is equivalent to an estate of about $100,000 to-day. I beseech the minister 'to raise this $5,000 limitation. From the point of view of administration his officers will get rid of a great deal of trouble, and, perhaps expensive trouble. How will the minister determine whether an estate is under or over $5,000? An estate of $5,001 pays a tax, while an estate of $4,999 pays no tax. The difficulty will be in arriving at a definite figure.
The valuation of a house might make all the difference.
Yes; it might depend upon some one small factor. I suggest that the limit is too low in any event.

It is just possible that the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John-Albert may be allowed to be shelved, but surely he has raised an important aspect of this question, and I rise, even at the risk of repetition, to support him, so that the matter may be impressed more forcibly upon the minister. Surely a man engaged in the merchant marine or serving on a convoy should be given every benefit that is contemplated by this section. One cannot help recalling the case of that brave man, Captain Fogarty Fegen. Under this section, if he was a Canadian, his family would derive nothing whatsoever. The Minister of National Revenue points out to me that the man may be in the naval reserve. I just took Captain Fogarty Fegen as an example. Undoubtedly there will be other cases. I strongly support the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John-Albert, which deserves every support it can receive.
What about this $5,000 limit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In a great majority of smaller estates the exemption on account of the widow and children would more than wipe out the estate.
That is a partial answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In cases where there are no widow and no dependent children, while there may be administrative difficulties, the beneficiaries, strangers for example, should pay a tax.
What about brothers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think they should.

I do not think so.
' Mr. ILSLEY: As I say, in the normal case, the exemptions will eliminate the problem.

Let me
give the minister an illustration. I have in my riding four brothers, all bachelors. None of them ever married. They have lived together, one doing one part of the work on a great big farm, and another, another. Under this section every one of them will pay, as they die, taxation on an estate of a little over $5,000 apiece, and when the last one dies, the whole thing will have gone to the government. I do not like the taste of it.

I would ask the minister to make the provision under subsection 3 as generous as possible. Under the Pension Act a person must qualify in a certain way and in a rather restrictive way, and something comes to them direct from the crown in return for their sacrifice or the sacrifice on the part of a loved one. But the provision here is not of that nature at all. It is merely to prevent the crown from benefiting unduly by the untimely death of some person who has lost his life on account of the war. Therefore I think the crown can afford to take a generous attitude. In Ontario the section allows the government to remove the whole duty if it sees fit. It is not specifically laid down except in those general terms, and I understand from the premier of Ontario that such cases will be liberally treated. Here the government should afford every relief possible to the heirs of a man who lost his life before his time in the great cause for which we are now fighting, and for that reason I would suggest that the provisions of the Pension Act can surely not be applicable. Although I am not at all familiar with them, they must be drawn far more strictly than in equity the provisions of this section should be drawn because the case is of such a different nature.
I would also specifically call attention to the item of 3 per cent. Three per cent would mean setting up quite a large sum which, accumulated at 3 per cent, would, after the expiration of the term of years, equal the amount of the tax. If you made it 4 per cent, which is much more reasonable, it would mean that a good deal smaller capital sum would have to be set up and paid now. The government should give every consideration to the heirs of men who meet their death before their time in this war, and I would strongly recommend 4 per cent, and, if the government had a generous turn of mind, 5 per cent. In these circumstances it would not be too much to ask that the estate go scot-free, but I realize that the minister would not go along

*Succession Duty Act
with me that far. But either 4 or 5 per cent rather than 3 per cent would be more in keeping with what the people of Canada would desire.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Three per cent is put in there because that is the existing market rate.

But the man who died did not want to make this investment to be improved at 3 per cent yearly. He has sacrificed his life for this country, and thereby the government comes into this tax on his estate before it ordinarily would. The government does not wrant to benefit by that fact. It wants to give him all the consideration it can, and it is quite likely that if he were investing his money he would not be content with 3 per cent but might need 4 or 5 per cent to maintain the family he leaves behind. I think that rather than have the government force the 3 per cent rate on him, they should give at least 4 if not 5 per cent. The minister will realize what a difference there is in the capital sum necessary now to be provided when the rate is 3 per cent compared with 4 or 5 per cent. The government should be extremely generous in these circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The section is standing
anyway.
Section stands.
On section 8-Allowances in computing aggregate net value and dutiable value.

May I call the minister's attention to paragraph (g) of subsection 2 dealing with duties paid elsewhere? This clause, of course, means that in any province where there are succession duties-and that applies to all of them-we pay a succession duty to the province at a high rate, and we pay a second duty to the federal authority at a relatively small rate, but no allowance whatever is made by the federal authority for the tax paid to the provincial authority.
As in income tax?

As in income tax. You are taxed on the tax you pay the province.
I call attention to another provision. For years in New Brunswick there has been a provision that life insurance may be taken out and assigned to the provincial treasurer earmarked, so to speak, for the payment of succession duties. To the extent that the duties are assessed and levied and paid out of that policy of life insurance, which, in many instances, has been placed for that specific purpose, there is no tax on that insurance. There is no tax to the extent that it is taken up by the assessment, and by doing
that you avoid the tax on a tax. It is a fair provision. Many people have already regulated their affairs to give effect to it, and I suggest that the minister ought to have some such principle in this bill, so that, for instance, a policy might be assigned, say, to the Receiver General of Canada under a provision similar to that which exists in some provincial statutes. He could make provision for this tax without having the estate liquidated, perhaps in a very difficult period. I know of no fund out of which succession duties are paid more easily than out of life insurance if one can afford to carry it. He might incorporate that principle and avoid' for his successors the tax on a tax; for that is what it amounts to.
By this section the government will take a tax on what my estate may have to pay to New Brunswick, or the estates of hon. gentlemen opposite may pay to some other province.
I suggest that double taxation has almost become a racket in this country. It is not fair. It cannot be justified on any basis of equity or common justice, and these two taxing authorities should get together, at least on this point, and give some consideration to the poor taxpayer. Everyone is defending the revenues of the country, but no one is saying a word for the taxpayer. This is not a war measure, I do not care what the minister says; it is an invasion of a field of the province and it could be got along without. I think the minister will find that, with the growing national income, many of the new taxes he has imposed, and some of those he has imposed since the budget began, will take up all the slack he needs. Surely he can exercise some leniency to the taxpayer so that he will not be taxed on a tax. That kind of taxation is an abomination. We have had it for years. I remember years ago when they put a tax on corporations on the same money that went to pay dividends to shareholders who paid income tax on that as well. The minister of the day, who is now sitting quietly in the other chamber, admitted the inequity of the thing but defended it on the theory that they needed money. The minister ought to give consideration to this plea, that the tax paid to a province should not be taxed by his department, and he should add a provision that if a person assigns insurance on his life, payable to take care of this tax, that should not be taxed. That is based on elements of common justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has
stated several times that there should not be any tax on a tax and that the proposition speaks for itself. I challenge that statement, and I put the simple case of the person who pays the tax on sugar. Everyone in the
Succession Duty Act,

country, I suppose, pays some part of the tax on sugar. The amount in the year is not very much. The average per individual is something like $1 on the one cent basis; it will be $2 on the two cent basis, and for the average family of five it will be, on that basis, $10. I am a householder buying sugar. I have an income. Out of my income I pay so much for sugar, and a tax of so much on that sugar; nevertheless I pay income tax on that same amount which I pay in the form of a tax on sugar. No one thinks that is shocking, but common sense or morals or logic would suggest-

The
analogy will not bear analysis. The position is not the same at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a simple way of disposing of the argument.
It will not dispose of it in my mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is simple and convincing. Let us take the person who is subject to two income taxes, one payable to a province and one to the dominion. That is shocking to the hon. gentleman, unless the taxpayer is allowed a deduction. The dominion does not allow, as a deduction from a person's income for income tax purposes, income tax he pays to the province. If I receive $100 in income and the province takes $10 and the dominion $10, what is there shocking about that? I have paid 20 per cent of my income, 10 per cent to one taxing authority and 10 per cent to the other. The hon. gentleman says that is a tax on a tax, because one of the jurisdictions-I do not know which one-does not allow the tax paid to the other jurisdiction as a deduction from income for income tax purposes. We have never allowed these income taxes as deductions, but some provinces do. Ontario allows the amount paid to the dominion as a deduction for income tax purposes, bu't some of the other provinces do not. I am applying here, in the Succession Duty Act, the same principle we have always applied in the income tax act. The theory of this is that the estate of a deceased owes two taxing authorities money. One authority takes a certain proportion, and the other authority, another. In a sense it is a tax on a tax, but in another sense it is merely two taxes on the same amount. Part of it goes to one authority and part to the other. Would it make the hon. gentleman feel any better if we took just as much as he paid to both authorities, that is, if we took as much as the total? Suppose the province went out of the field, and we took the amount paid to the province; we would not divide it into two parts and 
allow one part as a deduction before applying the tax on the rest. Yet the amount would be the same.

I will
counter that by reference to the national defence tax. That is a tax imposed at the source. We never get that money where it is taken beforehand, and yet we are taxed on it. Is there anything equitable in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is merely a matter of procedure.
It is a little more than procedure. It is a very important matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is exactly the same, as if a person received it and paid it back.
If he did not earn it, it would not be taxable.

Will the minister tell me why in section 1 it says "but not including the charges of solicitors"? That seems to be a debt as much as the rest- surrogate court fees, funeral expenses and so forth. Why not allow as a debt the solicitor's charges?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not a debt of the deceased, and it is capable of indefinite expansion.

Are surrogate
court fees a debt?
They are a tax. Surrogate court fees in my province are a tax paid by probate stamps. Allowance is made for deduction. I convict the minister on his own bill.
I think it is just as much a tax as anything else and should be allowed. I do not see any reason why it should not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If these surrogate court fees reach the dimensions of a succession duty we would not allow them.

I do not know what they are in other provinces, but during the Easter vacation I paid $904 to New Brunswick on an estate of just under $300,000. It was a substantial tax for the service rendered. It is a tax based on the gross value of the estate, not the net, because no deductions are allowed except for mortgages. Debts are not allowed to be deducted. It is an important item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The line is difficult to draw between a charge which is a fee and a charge which is really a tax.

Succession Duty Act

It started as a fee to cover a service, but has proved to be very profitable to the province. Every year for some years past they have carried into the revenue a substantial balance. It is not an important item, but is one with regard to which they always figure on having a credit balance. I cannot ask the minister to include solicitors' fees in the exemption; I do not think that would be fair because it would not be based on a principle. The principle of a deduction is that it is something existing or incurred by the death. You do not really have to have a solicitor to administer an estate.
You will have to now.

I take exception to that. I think you do have to have a solicitor, and it is a fee just the same as the surrogate court fees. I am not a solicitor. As I understand it, these solicitors' fees are taxed as well by the taxing officer.

"Taxing" there means
something different.
I still think it ought to be allowed as a deduction.
The leader of the opposition all day has been pointing out the severity of this particular bill-

No, I
have been dealing with the principle; I have raised no question about the rates.

The hon. gentleman's conclusion in his main speech and his successive observations to-day was, I understood, that this legislation is calculated to lead to the destruction of the system of free private enterprise and so forth.
Together with other taxes.

He has made the observation several times to-night, to which I do not remember the minister addressing himself, that this legislation is not for the purpose of raising money for the prosecution of the war.
I do not say that; I say it is not required for the prosecution of the war. The money could be obtained otherwise.

Apart from the permanency of this legislation, the minister does not say that at the end of the war he proposes to vacate this field, as he has said with respect to the invasion of other tax fields. Nevertheless I think we ought to have it clearly understood, having in mind the fact that the provinces legislate in this field that we are now 14873-205
entering, that this legislation does impose a measure of double taxation which in peace time it might be very difficult to justify. The minister should definitely say that he was persuaded to bring in this legislation because he had to find money to carry on the war and that, in his judgment and in the opinion of the government, this was regarded as a field which might well be explored for that purpose.

That
would be going beyond what he said in the budget speech.

I do not recall that, but
there ought to be some statement.
The hon. member wants a justification to use when he returns home.

I wish to make it clear that
we would not have brought in this measure if it had not been for the war and the need of money; but having once reached the point where we decided to introduce it, we do not introduce it as a temporary measure, for the reason stated in the budget speech:	It may
be that it will be repealed; it may be that my intentions about it or the intentions of this government will not necessarily govern permanently.
